Where it began

Roger Binny was born in Bengaluru on 19 July 1955 and went to school at Montfort School in Yercaud, St. Joseph's Indian High School and St. Germain High School. He was the first Anglo-Indian to play cricket for India. Before cricket took over he threw the javelin, and it left its mark: when he bowled, his front foot landed side-on to the crease rather than pointing down the pitch, a quirk no coaching manual would have taught him. He played his state cricket for Karnataka and was close to an India cap during his college years.

The player

Binny played 27 Tests for India between 1979 and 1987. His debut came in his home city, against Pakistan, and he took 47 wickets at 32.64 with two five-wicket hauls. With the bat he made 830 runs at 23.06, with five fifties and a best of 83 not out.

That 83 came against Pakistan in Bengaluru in 1983, when he and Madan Lal put on 155 for the seventh wicket, a record, to pull India out of trouble. His best bowling, 6 for 56 against Pakistan at Calcutta in 1987, included a burst of four wickets for nine runs in 30 balls. At Headingley in 1986 his seven wickets in the match helped India to a win in England. But the summer everyone remembers is 1983, when India won the World Cup and Binny's 18 wickets were the most by any bowler in the tournament. Two years later, in Australia, he was India's leading wicket-taker again as they won the World Championship of Cricket.

What made him special

He was the kind of cricketer a captain is glad to have. He took the shine off the new ball so the spinners could get to work, he hit hard and stubbornly down the order when a match needed saving, and as a tall, athletic man he was a fine fielder. He came in and out of the side over the years, and his Test figures are honest rather than dazzling, but give him an English sky and a one-day final and he was hard to keep out of the game.

Away from the middle

Binny went on to coach. He was in charge of the India Under-19 side that won the Under-19 World Cup in Sri Lanka in 2000, a team that included Mohammed Kaif and Yuvraj Singh, and later worked with the Under-16s, where Ambati Rayudu, Robin Uthappa and Irfan Pathan came through. He also served as a national selector, ran the Karnataka State Cricket Association, and in October 2022 was elected president of the Indian board, the 36th person to hold the post. His son Stuart Binny also played for Karnataka and for India. In the film 83, about the World Cup win, he was played by Nishant Dahiya.

And finally

Plenty of bowlers are told their action looks odd. Very few can say it came from throwing a javelin, and fewer still can point to a World Cup winner's medal as proof that it worked.
